title: TCP/IP internetworking from heterogeneous packet networks to the 1983 operational transition
pressure: Packet networks existed but used incompatible host/network assumptions; communication had to work across independently administered heterogeneous networks.
preExistingWorldModel: ARPANET NCP worked inside one network, while radio/satellite/local networks had different packet sizes, loss, delay and administration.
candidateRoutes: replace all networks with one universal network
end-to-end internetwork protocol over heterogeneous networks
observationsAndInstruments: Cerf/Kahn work separated internetworking from any single underlying network.
TCP experimentation led to separation of IP datagrams from end-to-end transport.
Demonstrations linked packet radio, satellite and ARPANET.
The 1 January 1983 conversion moved operational ARPANET hosts from NCP to TCP/IP.
decisiveTests: route across multiple packet technologies without assuming one link behavior
technicalOrScientificTransition: The Internet emerged from an architecture tolerant of heterogeneous local networks plus a long operational transition of implementations, addressing, naming and institutions.
rivalsAndFailures: NCP was useful inside ARPANET but insufficient for internetworking.
A strong protocol without deployable host software and transition operations would not create an Internet.
Later OSI competition showed formal international standardization alone did not guarantee deployment.
diffusionAndScaling: Diffusion depended on complements, cost/yield/standards and institutional adoption; the nominal breakthrough date did not equal broad effective use.
standardsAndInstitutions: Laboratories, firms, standard bodies, regulators, users and infrastructure operators owned different parts of evidence, implementation and consequence.
externalitiesAndCorrections: Lifecycle harms and authority changes are preserved where evidenced rather than inferred from local technical success.
secondOrderEffects: The Internet emerged from an architecture tolerant of heterogeneous local networks plus a long operational transition of implementations, addressing, naming and institutions.
sourceNativeSummary: The Internet emerged from an architecture tolerant of heterogeneous local networks plus a long operational transition of implementations, addressing, naming and institutions.
unresolvedHistoricalQuestions: Which complement most constrained diffusion at each lifecycle phase?
Which later narrative compresses materially distributed work?
